title: Throughput & Isolation Buying Framework
content:
Purpose: short working playbook for GTM, sales engineering, and proposition owners to position Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) to procurement and platform teams focused on predictable throughput, tenant isolation, and SLA-backed economics. This is intentionally pragmatic: buyer objections + suggested language + procurement checklist + sample clause snippets for legal/commercial teams.

Audience: sales reps (AE), solutions engineers (SE), platform architects, procurement buyers, legal deal desk.

Background / why this doc: we keep hearing 3 buyer anxieties that block deals: 1) unpredictable performance under bursty load, 2) noisy-neighbor risk (data isolation & QoS), 3) procurement/legal wanting clear, auditable SLOs and remediation. This playbook translates technical differentiation into procurement-ready artifacts.

Elevator (one-liner): Redwood Dedicated delivers predictable inference throughput with SLA-backed isolation so platform teams can deploy latency-sensitive LLM features without building and operating GPU fleets.

Positioning pillars (how to lead):
- Predictable unit economics: commit + predictable utilization -> stable per-token costs. Pitch: “Reserved throughput lets you budget inference like infra: predictable cost per request, even at scale.”
- Latency & tail guarantees: provide measurable P50/P95/P99 latency SLOs across slot configurations and sequence profiles; tie to credits/remedy. Pitch: “We guarantee the tail so UX-critical flows stay snappy.”
- Isolation for compliance & QoS: dedicated pools mapped to tenancy boundaries (team, product, customer) with KPIs. Pitch: “No noisy neighbors — capacity is isolated and measurable.”
- Procurement-ready remediation: simple escalation ladder, credits, and committed capacity add-ons so procurement can quantify vendor risk.

Buyer personas & tuned messages:
- Platform Architect (technical): cares about latency stability, autoscale behavior, and integration surface. Message: explain per-route SLAs, input/output size assumptions, KV-cache behavior, and how canary rollouts work across model variants. Provide architecture diagram and expected throughput numbers for 8k/32k seqs.
- Procurement / Ops Buyer: cares about contract remedies, terminology, service credits, measurement windows. Message: provide concrete SLA language, measurement docs, runbook for incident remediation, and a handoff packet to legal.
- CTO / VP Eng (economic): cares about unit economics and lock-in risk. Message: show cost projection vs. pay-as-you-go + ops uplift vs. self-hosting (capex & headcount), and describe downgrade/exit paths (snapshot/export capabilities).

Common objections & suggested rebuttals (short):
- Objection: “We’ve seen vendor endpoints throttle unpredictably during peak.”
  Rebuttal: Describe autoscale burst policies, minimum reserved throughput, and fallback routing to compatible model variants. Offer a 30-day load validation window and an SLO-backed pilot.
- Objection: “How do you define isolation? Are VMs/GPU hosts shared?”
  Rebuttal: Explain dedicated GPU pools, tenancy mapping, and isolation metrics (host allocation ratios, memory/KV cache partitioning). Offer an on-prem or VPC deployment for fully customer-managed control plane.
- Objection: “What happens if we exceed committed throughput?”
  Rebuttal: Show staged overage behavior: short bursts allowed, soft throttling + surge credits, and optional burst add-on capacity that triggers automatically (configurable). Clarify pricing anchors for overage and how to negotiate surge inclusion.
- Objection: “We need auditable proofs for compliance.”
  Rebuttal: Point to audit logs, per-request traces, token-level cost breakdowns in Console, and integrations with KMS/HSM for key handling. Offer SOC2 / ISO artifacts and a data flow diagram.

Procurement playbook (step-by-step):
1) Commercial anchor: propose a three-tier commitment (base reserved throughput, surge buffer, on-demand cap) with clear per-unit pricing for each band. Include a 6–12 month lookback for true-up.
2) SLAs to negotiate: uptime for control plane (if hosted), P95/P99 latency SLOs per route, and guaranteed minimum throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec for specified sequence length).
3) Remedies: primary: service credits as % of monthly fee; secondary: termination-rights tied to repeated SLA breaches (3+ within 90 days) with phased exit support.
4) Proof window: 30–60 day validation in prod sandbox with telemetry-sharing and joint ops reviews.
5) Legal handoff: include sample SLA appendix (see snippets below), runbook references, and a schedule for monthly SRE review meetings.

SLA / contract snippets (pickup language — draftable for legal):
- Scope: “This SLA applies to Redwood Dedicated capacity provisioned by Customer and covers the inference serving endpoints and associated control plane services agreed in Schedule A.”
- Uptime: “Redwood shall maintain a monthly Control Plane Availability of 99.9% measured across regional control plane endpoints, excluding scheduled maintenance with 48h notice.”
- Throughput floor: “Redwood guarantees a minimum sustained inference throughput of X tokens/sec (or Y requests/sec for sequences <= Z tokens) for the committed capacity during each billing period. Measurement is performed at the routing edge before batching.”
- Latency SLO: “For requests with sequence length <= 4k tokens, average P95 latency shall be <= 220ms and P99 latency shall be <= 480ms under normal operating conditions (excluding scheduled maintenance).”
- Remedies: “If Redwood fails to meet the Throughput or Latency SLOs in any monthly measurement window, Customer shall receive a service credit equal to 5% of the monthly Dedicated fee for each SLO missed, capped at 50% for that month. Three or more missed monthly SLOs in any consecutive 90-day window shall entitle Customer to termination for convenience with a 60-day transition assistance period.”
- Isolation definition: "Isolation refers to logical and physical allocation of GPU capacity (pools, node allocation), KV-cache partitioning, and request routing ensuring no cross-tenant KV cache eviction policies occur between designated tenant pools. Where Customer requires physical host allocation, Redwood will provide VPC-private or on-prem deployment options."

Competitive notes (short matrix prose):
- Public cloud managed endpoint: usually lower operational effort but shared noisy-neighbor risk and less predictable tail latency; pricing often opaque for large sustained workloads. Redwood differentiates with reserved pools + predictable unit economics + tooling for per-route telemetry.
- Pure self-host / infra build: offers ultimate control but high capex and ops lift (SRE hiring, GPU procurement, model ops). Redwood reduces time-to-market and OPEX while allowing private deployments for regulated workloads.
- Other inference vendors: many offer reserved capacity, but few pair strong observability and clear remediation language. Call out: our baking in of KV caching and routing fallbacks, and per-token telemetry as commercial differentiators.

Commercial levers & negotiation play:
- Offer a 6–8 week pilot with a reduced reserved commitment to prove tail behavior. Use performance data to firm up final committed throughput.
- Use a two-year pricing ladder with an option to increase reserved throughput at pre-agreed tiers; incentivize longer commitment with lower per-token rates.
- Include an SLA premium tier (SLA+): higher credits, quarterly performance review, and a CX/SE named contact for prioritized incident response.

Operational onboarding checklist (what SE provides to buyer):
- Capacity sizing worksheet (expected RPS, token size distribution, burst patterns).
- Integration checklist (auth, routing, model pinning, fallback policies).
- Runbook & escalation flow (SE/Reliability contact roster, on-call windows, SLAs for incident responses).
- Measurement artifact: template for shared telemetry export (CSV/JSON) and dashboard links for legal to audit SLOs.

Sample email to procurement (one-paragraph):
Subject: Redwood Dedicated — throughput & isolation proposal
Hi [Procurement lead],
Following our discussion, attached is a short commercial sketch for Dedicated capacity. In summary: a reserved throughput commitment backed by latency & throughput SLOs, explicit isolation guarantees, and a 30–60 day validation window. We propose a two-band pricing model (base reserved + surge buffer) and a standard SLA appendix with service-credit remedies. Happy to sync to walk through specifics and map to your procurement timelines.

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Decide default numbers for Throughput floor (example: baseline 20k tokens/sec for a 4-GPU pool) — need SRE sizing input.
- Finalize latency targets per sequence length (4k vs 32k) — alignment with Serving Runtime team.
- Confirm legal’s appetite for termination-after-3-SLA-breaches clause — get input from deal desk.

Notes to self / SE handoff: keep this doc lean and convert into a two-page one-pager + SLA appendix for legal. Create a template slide for platform architects (diagram + numbers) and a procurement packet (SLA appendix, runbook, pricing ladder) to attach to proposals.

Appendix: quick sizing example (informal)
- Customer X traffic: 200 reqs/sec average, 5% peaks to 800 reqs/sec, avg seq size 600 tokens. Recommendation: reserve capacity equal to ~50% of peak (to lower cost) + 20% surge buffer. Pilot phase: run with 40% reserved and measure KV cache hit rates; escalate to final commit after 30d.

End.
